## 👋 Welcome

This is a **hands-on introduction to doing AI on supercomputers**. It starts from
the ground up (the shell, Python, and how HPC systems work) and builds all the
way to **training large language models across many GPUs**. Almost every page is a
runnable notebook: you can read it here, open it in Google Colab, or run it on an
HPC system.

::: {.callout-tip title="🎯 Who this is for" collapse="false"}
Students and researchers who are **new to AI, HPC, or both**. You don't need prior
machine-learning experience. Comfort with basic programming helps, but the first
few pages ([Using Python](./00-intro-AI-HPC/3-python/),
[Working with Data](./00-intro-AI-HPC/4-data/)) bring you up to speed.
:::

### 🚦 Start here

Work through the five parts in order. Each builds on the last:

1. **[\[0\] Intro to AI and HPC](00-intro-AI-HPC/)** — compute systems, the
   scheduler, Python, and data; then your first models (Monte Carlo, linear
   regression, clustering). **New? [Start with Compute Systems ➡️](./00-intro-AI-HPC/0-compute-systems/)**
2. **[\[1\] Neural Networks](01-neural-networks/)** — from a single neuron to
   CNNs, representation learning, and distributed training.
3. **[\[2\] Large Language Models](02-llms/)** — how LLMs work, then build and
   train a GPT from scratch and learn to evaluate it.
4. **[\[3\] Advanced / Large-Scale LLMs](03-advanced-llms/)** — MoE, pretraining
   at scale, fault tolerance, post-training, and RL for reasoning.
5. **[\[4\] AI for Science](04-ai-for-science/)** — the payoff: the same
   Transformer + HPC stack applied to genomes, proteins, and molecules.

::: {.callout-note title="🖥️ Where the code runs" collapse="false"}
The lighter notebooks run anywhere (including a laptop or **Google Colab**; look
for the [![](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com)
badge at the top of each page). The large-scale training examples are meant for an
HPC system. The bootcamp uses **Jupyter on [NERSC Perlmutter](https://docs.nersc.gov/systems/perlmutter/)**
(project `m4388`), but the commands are scheduler-agnostic and work on ALCF PBS
systems too. See [running instructions](#running-instructions) below.
:::

## 🏔️ Running instructions {#running-instructions}

### 🔬 On Perlmutter (NERSC) {#nersc}

This is the machine we use during the bootcamp.

::: {.callout-important title="📦 Nothing to install"}
Every package these notebooks need — `torch` (CUDA), `transformers`, `ezpz`,
`bootcamp`, `plotly`, `nltk`, `bertviz` — is already in a shared conda
environment that all of `m4388` can read:

```
/global/cfs/cdirs/m4388/envs/intro-hpc-bootcamp
```

You **do not** run `pip install`, `conda create`, or `uv` anything. Clone the
notebooks, point Jupyter at the kernel, and start working.
:::

**1. Get the notebooks.** From a Perlmutter terminal
([jupyter.nersc.gov](https://jupyter.nersc.gov) → *Perlmutter Login Node* →
**Terminal**, or `ssh <user>@perlmutter.nersc.gov`):

```bash
# your own directory inside the project space -- do NOT work in a shared clone,
# and do not edit someone else's
mkdir -p /global/cfs/cdirs/m4388/projects/project8/$USER
cd       /global/cfs/cdirs/m4388/projects/project8/$USER

git clone https://github.com/saforem2/intro-hpc-bootcamp
cd intro-hpc-bootcamp
```

You now have your own copy to edit and break freely. `$SCRATCH` or `$HOME` work
just as well if you would rather keep it there — nothing below depends on where
the clone lives.

**2. Make the shared kernel visible.** One-time setup, then log out and back
into Jupyter so the file is re-read:

```bash
echo 'export JUPYTER_PATH=/global/cfs/cdirs/m4388' >> ~/.bashrc
```

**3. Open a notebook and pick the kernel.** In the Jupyter file browser, open
any `content/**/index.ipynb`, then choose the kernel:

> **Intro to HPC Bootcamp**

That environment already has `torch` (CUDA), `transformers`, `ezpz`, `bootcamp`,
`plotly`, `nltk`, `bertviz`, and the rest of the stack these pages import.

::: {.callout-tip title="🐚 Using it from a terminal instead of Jupyter" collapse="true"}
Same environment, activated by hand — useful for `ezpz test`, batch scripts, or
anything you want to `srun`:

```bash
module load conda
conda activate /global/cfs/cdirs/m4388/envs/intro-hpc-bootcamp

ezpz test          # sanity-check the distributed setup
```

For a GPU node, grab an allocation first:

```bash
salloc --nodes 1 --qos interactive --time 01:00:00 \
       --constraint gpu --account m4388
```
:::

::: {.callout-note title="🧯 If something goes wrong" collapse="true"}
| symptom | fix |
|:--|:--|
| Kernel **Intro to HPC Bootcamp** not in the menu | `JUPYTER_PATH` not set, or you have not logged out/in since setting it (step 2) |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'bootcamp'` (or `ezpz`) | You are on a different kernel — check the kernel name in the top-right of the notebook |
| `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED` on a dataset download | The env sets `SSL_CERT_FILE` on activation; if you launched python without activating, run `export SSL_CERT_FILE=$CONDA_PREFIX/ssl/cert.pem` |
| `OSError: [Errno 524]` from a 🤗 download | `$HOME` is GPFS and does not support file locking. `export HF_HOME=$SCRATCH/.cache/huggingface` **before** importing `transformers` |
:::

### 💻 Off the cluster (not needed for the bootcamp)

*Bootcamp participants can skip this — the shared environment above covers
everything.* These pages also run on a laptop or in Colab if you want to keep
working after the week is over, or you do not have an `m4388` allocation.

Easiest is the
[![](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com)
badge at the top of any page: those notebooks install what they need in their
first cell. To run locally instead:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/saforem2/intro-hpc-bootcamp
cd intro-hpc-bootcamp
python3 -m pip install -e .                                   # the `bootcamp` helpers
python3 -m pip install "git+https://github.com/saforem2/ezpz" # distributed utilities
```

## 🌐 Distributed Training Example {#distributed-training-example}

Ready to train a real model across multiple GPUs? The full end-to-end
walkthrough (request an interactive job, set up the environment, and launch a
multi-node run with [`ezpz launch`](https://github.com/saforem2/ezpz)) lives on
the dedicated pages, complete with annotated output:

- 🧠 **[\[1.4\] Distributed Training](./01-neural-networks/4-distributed-training/)** —
  the concepts (DDP, FSDP, collective ops, 3D parallelism) *and* a complete
  Perlmutter run you can reproduce, including a full annotated training log.
- 🚀 **[\[2.1\] Parallel Training](./02-llms/1-parallel-training/)** — the same
  ideas applied to pretraining a GPT with [`wordplay`](https://github.com/saforem2/wordplay).

::: {.callout-tip title="TL;DR: launch a run" collapse="true"}
On an HPC system with an interactive allocation:

```bash
# 1. set up the environment (system-agnostic; on Perlmutter just activate the
#    shared env instead -- see the step-by-step below)
source <(curl -fsSL https://bit.ly/ezpz-utils) && ezpz_setup_env
uv pip install "git+https://github.com/saforem2/ezpz"

# 2. verify the distributed setup
ezpz test

# 3. launch 2D-parallel training (auto-detects SLURM srun / PBS mpiexec)
ezpz launch python3 -m ezpz.examples.fsdp_tp --model small --tp 2 --train-iters 100
```
:::

<!-- moved: the full step-by-step + annotated training log now lives in
     01-neural-networks/4-distributed-training (canonical), to keep the home
     page focused on orientation. -->

<details closed><summary><h3>Full step-by-step (Perlmutter)</h3></summary>

This runs a **2D-parallel** (tensor/sequence parallel + FSDP) training job on a
Llama-style model, straight out of `ezpz` — no repo to clone and nothing to
install, since `ezpz` is already in the shared environment.

1. Login to Perlmutter:

    ```bash
    ssh <user>@perlmutter.nersc.gov
    ```

1. Request an interactive job (4 A100s per node, charged to the GPU account
   `m4388_g`):

    ```bash
    NODES=2 ; HRS=02 ; QUEUE=interactive
    salloc --nodes $NODES --qos $QUEUE --time $HRS:30:00 \
           -C 'gpu' --gpus=$(( 4 * NODES )) -A m4388_g
    ```

1. Activate the shared environment:

    ```bash
    module load conda
    conda activate /global/cfs/cdirs/m4388/envs/intro-hpc-bootcamp
    ```

1. Verify the distributed setup before spending an allocation on a real run:

    ```bash
    ezpz test
    ```

    `ezpz` discovers the job from SLURM, so you should see one line per rank and
    a `WORLD_SIZE` equal to your total GPU count (8 for the 2-node job above).

1. Launch 2D-parallel training:

    ```bash
    ezpz launch python3 -m ezpz.examples.fsdp_tp \
        --model small \
        --tp 2 \
        --dataset random \
        --seq-len 1024 \
        --batch-size 8 \
        --train-iters 100
    ```

    `ezpz launch` auto-detects the scheduler (SLURM → `srun`, PBS → `mpiexec`)
    and fills in the rank/host bookkeeping, so there is no `srun -n $NGPUS` to
    get wrong.

::: {.callout-tip title="🎛️ What the flags mean" collapse="true"}
| flag | meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `--tp 2` | tensor-parallel degree. Must divide `WORLD_SIZE`; the remaining ranks (`WORLD_SIZE / tp`) become the FSDP data-parallel dimension. With 8 GPUs and `--tp 2` you get 2-way TP × 4-way FSDP. |
| `--model small` | size preset (`debug`, `small`, `medium`, `large`, `xl`, …) instead of setting `--dim`/`--n-layers` by hand. Start at `debug` if you just want it to finish fast. |
| `--dataset random` | synthetic tokens, so there is no dataset download or filesystem I/O. Swap in any HuggingFace repo id to train on real text. |
| `--batch-size 8` | *per-DP-rank* micro-batch. Global batch = `--batch-size × (WORLD_SIZE / --tp)`. |

Other flags worth knowing: `--activation-checkpoint` to trade compute for
memory, `--compile` for `torch.compile`, and `--pytorch-profiler` if you want a
trace. Run `python3 -m ezpz.examples.fsdp_tp --help` for the full list.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="📈 Try scaling it" collapse="true"}
The interesting exercise is watching what changes as you vary the parallelism
*without* changing the model:

```bash
# same 8 GPUs, three different splits of TP vs FSDP
ezpz launch python3 -m ezpz.examples.fsdp_tp --model small --tp 1 --train-iters 50
ezpz launch python3 -m ezpz.examples.fsdp_tp --model small --tp 2 --train-iters 50
ezpz launch python3 -m ezpz.examples.fsdp_tp --model small --tp 4 --train-iters 50
```

More TP means less memory per GPU but more communication per step. Where the
crossover lands depends on your model size and interconnect — which is exactly
the tradeoff [\[3.1\] Pretraining at Scale](./03-advanced-llms/1-pretraining-at-scale/)
works through.
:::

</details>
